findings.title: run command repo field has no length cap in parseCommand
findings.detail: The sprint_goal case received a repo length cap (AUDIT-IFleet-c8d40f35, fixed 2026-08-02) but the sibling `case 'run':` block at line 431 was missed. It assigns parsed.repo directly with no length check: `if (typeof parsed.repo === 'string') cmd.repo = parsed.repo;`. An attacker with a valid HMAC secret can supply an arbitrarily long repo string that propagates into store writes and RepoResolver allow-list checks.
findings.fix_sketch: Add `if (parsed.repo.length > 256) throw new Error('run: repo exceeds maximum length');` immediately after the typeof check in the run case, mirroring the sprint_goal fix.
findings.fix_summary: Added length guard matching sprint_goal pattern.

findings.title: postDiscordAlert URL parsing inside Promise executor creates unhandled rejection on malformed URL
findings.detail: In src/orchestrator/index.ts, postDiscordAlert() constructs `new Promise((resolve) => { const url = new URL(webhookUrl); ... })`. The executor only has a resolve parameter — no reject. If webhookUrl is malformed, `new URL()` throws synchronously inside the executor, and in Node.js 15+ a throw inside a Promise constructor with no reject handler produces an unhandled rejection that crashes the daemon process.
findings.fix_sketch: Parse the URL outside the Promise constructor with a try/catch. On parse failure, return Promise.resolve() after logging a warning. This prevents the unhandled rejection while still surfacing the bad config.
findings.fix_summary: Moved URL parsing before the Promise constructor with try/catch guard.

findings.title: AnthropicCompleter complete has no timeout or AbortSignal — can hang indefinitely
findings.detail: In src/agents/proposer/candidate-gen.ts, AnthropicCompleter.complete() calls `this.fetchImpl(ANTHROPIC_ENDPOINT, { ... })` with no AbortController or signal. If the Anthropic API is slow, degraded, or unresponsive, the nightly Proposer run hangs permanently with no timeout. The daemon does not have a per-run timeout for the Proposer either, so a single hung fetch blocks all nightly proposal generation forever.
findings.fix_sketch: Create an AbortController with a reasonable timeout (e.g. 60 s), pass its signal to fetch, and throw a TimeoutError if it fires. Wire the timeout through the completer interface so callers can override it.
findings.fix_summary: Added 60s AbortController timeout to the fetch call.

findings.title: spawnCapture has no timeout — git operations can hang indefinitely
findings.detail: packages/orchestrator-core/src/repos/manager.ts spawnCapture() spawns a git subprocess with no kill timeout. A git clone or fetch to a slow or unresponsive remote will hold the Promise forever. Since git operations (ensureClone, allocateWorktree) run in the tick-loop critical path, a single hung clone stalls all subsequent task dispatch for that repo.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a `timeoutMs` parameter to spawnCapture (default: 120_000). Use `child.kill('SIGTERM')` in a setTimeout, then SIGKILL after a short grace period if still alive. Reject the promise with a descriptive TimeoutError.

findings.title: reviewer worker role gets acceptEdits permission mode instead of viewOnly — violates least privilege
findings.detail: In packages/orchestrator-core/src/workers/claude.ts, buildClaudeArgs() hardcodes `--permission-mode acceptEdits` for all worker roles including the reviewer. The reviewer only needs to read the diff and output a JSON verdict; it has no legitimate reason to write files. With acceptEdits, a jailbroken reviewer can use Edit/Write tools to modify worktree files, potentially injecting code before the PR is opened.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a permissionMode field to SpawnOpts (default: 'acceptEdits') and pass it through buildClaudeArgs. The factory's spawn call for the reviewer role should pass permissionMode: 'viewOnly'.

findings.title: withLock passes fn as both resolve and reject handler — misleading but functionally equivalent
findings.detail: In packages/orchestrator-core/src/repos/manager.ts line 182, `prev.then(fn, fn)` passes the same zero-argument function as both onFulfilled and onRejected. When the previous lock rejects, JavaScript passes the rejection reason as an argument to fn() — but since fn() ignores all arguments, the behavior is identical to `prev.then(fn, () => fn())`. The expression is misleading because it implies fn() is called with the rejection reason, but it actually runs the lock function unconditionally regardless of rejection type.
findings.fix_sketch: Change `prev.then(fn, fn)` to `prev.then(fn, () => fn())` to make the intent explicit: run fn regardless of whether the previous lock succeeded or failed.
findings.fix_summary: Changed prev.then(fn, fn) to prev.then(fn, () => fn()) for clarity.
